notes.meaning: All people across the earth are called to shout out with joy to the Lord as their King. This summons looks beyond Israel and invites every nation to honor the true God. When people everywhere hear the good news of God, they can join together in this glad shout.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine explained this joyful shout as an overflowing gladness of heart that words cannot fully express, comparing it to the cheerful shouts of workers during the harvest.

notes.meaning: God's people are told to serve Him with gladness and to come into His presence with joyful singing. Serving God is not meant to feel like heavy or bitter slavery, because He is a loving and gracious Master. True worship fills our hearts with cheerfulness as we praise Him together.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine taught that this service holds no bitterness because believers are both God's servants and set free by His love, allowing the conscience to rejoice along with the voice.

notes.meaning: Worshippers are reminded to recognize that the Lord alone is God, the Creator who made us and owns us. He claims us as His own flock, guarding and feeding us just as a shepherd tends sheep in a pasture. Because our lives come from Him, we can safely trust His tender care.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine interpreted the statement that the Lord is God as pointing to Jesus Christ, showing that the One who was scourged and crucified is Himself the divine Creator.

notes.meaning: The psalm invites worshippers to enter the temple gates and courtyards with thanksgiving and praise. While this originally referred to the courts of the temple in Jerusalem, it calls all people into shared public worship. Entering God's presence is a high privilege that deserves our deepest gratitude.

The psalm closes with the reasons to praise God: He is good, His loving devotion lasts forever, and His faithfulness never fails. His kindness is not temporary, but continues without end through every generation. We can be confident in Him because He always keeps His word.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine taught that God's mercy does not stop once He frees us from sin, but continues to protect and guide believers all the way into eternal life.
